Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov.description: The youngest Karamazov brother, commonly known as Alyosha. A gentle and spiritual novice at the monastery under the guidance of Father Zossima, he serves as the moral center of the novel.

Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov.description: Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov is the father of Dmitri, Ivan, and Alexey. He is a landowner notorious for his greed, debauchery, and neglectful behavior.

Dmitri.description: The eldest son of Fyodor Pavlovitch, a former officer known for his emotional instability and the primary defendant in his father's murder trial.

Adelaïda Ivanovna.description: Fyodor Pavlovitch's first wife and mother of Dmitri, who came from the noble Miüsov family.

Petersburg.description: A major Russian city (now called Saint Petersburg), often associated with culture, education, and political life.

district.description: Refers to the local administrative region or area in which the Karamazovs live.

province.description: A larger administrative region in Russia, encompassing several districts.

landowner.description: A person who owns land, especially a member of the rural gentry in 19th-century Russia.

toady.description: A person who flatters or ingratiates themselves with someone powerful for personal gain.

dowry.description: Property or money brought by a bride to her husband upon marriage.

deed of conveyance.description: A legal document that transfers ownership of property from one person to another.

orgies.description: Wild, excessive parties, often involving heavy drinking and immoral behavior.

harem.description: A group of women associated with one man, often used to describe a man's household of concubines or mistresses.

divinity student.description: A student studying theology, typically preparing for a career in the church.

garret.description: A small, often cramped attic room, typically inhabited by poor people.

typhus.description: A serious infectious disease caused by bacteria, often spread by lice or fleas, common in the 19th century.

caprice.description: A sudden and unaccountable change of mood or behavior.

buffoon.description: A ridiculous but amusing person; a clown.

runaway bride.description: A bride who leaves her husband or fiancé, often suddenly and unexpectedly.

promotion.description: An advancement in rank or position, often used here ironically.

emancipation.description: The process of being set free from legal, social, or political restrictions; liberation.

Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov.description: Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov is a wealthy, cultured landowner and distant relative of the Karamazovs, known for his liberal views and European culture.

Moscow.description: The capital city of Russia, where Mitya's grandmother and later a cousin reside.

Paris.description: The capital of France, where Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov lives for many years.

Proudhon.description: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, a French philosopher and socialist whom Miüsov claims to have known.

Bakunin.description: Mikhail Bakunin, a Russian revolutionary anarchist, also known personally by Miüsov.

Paris Revolution of February 1848.description: A significant historical event in France, part of the broader European revolutions of 1848, referenced by Miüsov.

Caucasus.description: A region at the border of Europe and Asia, where Dmitri Fyodorovitch serves in the military.

debauchery.description: Excessive indulgence in sensual pleasures; moral corruption.

souls.description: An archaic Russian term for serfs or peasants, used to count the population of an estate.

gymnasium.description: A type of secondary school in Russia and Europe, providing advanced academic education.

clericals.description: A term referring to members of the clergy or those associated with the church, often used pejoratively by secular or liberal critics.

doles.description: Small amounts of money given out, often as charity or allowance.

installments.description: Partial payments made over time towards a total sum owed.

Sofya Ivanovna.description: Fyodor Pavlovitch's second wife, a meek and gentle orphan who suffers greatly in her marriage and is the mother of Ivan and Alexey.

Yefim Petrovitch Polenov.description: The Marshal of Nobility of the province and principal heir of the general's widow, who takes responsibility for Ivan and Alexey's upbringing.

Eye-Witness.description: The pseudonym under which Ivan publishes newspaper articles.

Marshal of Nobility.description: A provincial official responsible for representing the interests of the local nobility in Russia.

ecclesiastical courts.description: Church courts in Russia responsible for religious and some civil matters, often a subject of public debate.

novice.description: A person who has entered a monastery and is preparing to become a monk but has not yet taken final vows.

benefactress.description: A woman who gives help, especially financial aid, to another person.

halter.description: A noose or rope for hanging, here referring to a suicide attempt.

profligate.description: A person given to wildly extravagant and immoral living.

possessed by devils.description: A phrase describing a state of hysteria or mental illness, believed to be caused by demonic possession in Russian folk belief.

cassock.description: A long, close-fitting garment worn by members of the clergy or those in religious orders.

legacy.description: Money or property left to someone in a will.

retainers.description: Servants or attendants, especially in a wealthy household.

Mother of God.description: The Mother of God, also known as the Virgin Mary, Madonna, or Our Lady, is the mother of Jesus Christ and is venerated in Orthodox Christianity as an intercessor, protector, and ideal of spiritual purity.
aliases: Image of the Mother of God

Italy.description: A country in Southern Europe, referenced here as the destination of Yefim Petrovitch's widow and family.

Odessa.description: A port city in southern Ukraine (then part of the Russian Empire), where Fyodor Pavlovitch lived for a period.

Jews.description: Refers to the Jewish community, mentioned in the context of Fyodor Pavlovitch's social circle in Odessa.

monks.description: Men who have taken religious vows and live in a monastery, central to Orthodox Christian practice.

hermitage.description: A secluded part of the monastery where the elder Zossima resides, often reserved for spiritual elders.

requiems.description: Religious services or prayers for the dead, performed for the repose of souls in Orthodox Christianity.

saint.description: A holy person recognized by the Church, often venerated with icons and candles.

our town cemetery.description: The local burial ground in the Karamazovs' town, where Alyosha's mother is buried.

our monastery.description: The specific local monastery near the Karamazovs' town, central to Alyosha's spiritual journey.

the monks' wives.description: A colloquial and somewhat scandalous term for women living near a monastery, rumored to have relationships with monks.

French women.description: Referenced in contrast to Russian women, alluding to perceived differences in culture or reputation.

Lutheran.description: Relating to Lutheranism, a branch of Protestant Christianity, used here to suggest a more 'enlightened' or less traditional view of hell.

elder.description: A senior monk in the Orthodox tradition, often revered for wisdom and spiritual guidance.

image.description: In this context, a religious icon or painting, typically of Christ, the Virgin Mary, or a saint, used in Orthodox Christian worship.

lamp.description: A devotional lamp, often kept burning before an icon in Orthodox homes and churches.

benefactor.description: A person who provides support, often financial, to another, especially in the context of patronage.

provincial gymnasium.description: A secondary school in the Russian Empire, providing classical education to boys.

pawn.description: To pledge an item as security for a loan, often at a pawnshop.

fasts.description: Periods of abstaining from certain foods or pleasures for religious reasons, observed by Orthodox Christians.

harlots.description: A derogatory term for prostitutes or promiscuous women.

miracles.description: Miracles are supernatural events considered to be acts of God, often associated with saints or holy figures in religious tradition.

Apostle Thomas.description: One of the twelve apostles of Jesus, known for doubting Jesus's resurrection until he saw him; referenced as a symbol of faith and doubt.

God.description: The supreme being in Christian theology, central to the faith and spiritual life of the characters.

immortality.description: The belief in the eternal existence of the soul after death, a key concept in Christian doctrine.

socialism.description: A political and economic theory advocating for collective or governmental ownership and administration of the means of production and distribution of goods; here, it is associated with atheism.

tower of Babel.description: A biblical story symbolizing human pride and the attempt to build a society without God.

mass.description: A Christian religious service, especially in the Orthodox and Catholic traditions, involving the Eucharist.

Sinai.description: Mount Sinai, a significant location in Christian and Jewish tradition, known for its monasteries.

Athos.description: A monastic peninsula in Greece, home to many Orthodox monasteries and elders.

Tartars.description: A group of Turkic-speaking peoples whose invasions affected Russian history, referenced here as a historical calamity.

Constantinople.description: The historic capital of the Byzantine Empire (now Istanbul), significant in Orthodox Christianity.

Kozelski Optin Monastery.description: A famous Russian Orthodox monastery known for its tradition of elders (startsy).

relics.description: Physical remains or personal effects of a saint, venerated in religious tradition for their association with holiness.

ikons.description: Religious images or icons, especially in the Eastern Orthodox Church, believed to be windows to the divine.

novitiate.description: The period or state of being a novice, especially in a religious order, involving training and probation.

obedience.description: A monastic vow or practice of submitting one's will to a superior or elder.

Syria.description: A country in the Middle East, referenced as the location of an early Christian monastery.

Egypt.description: A country in North Africa, referenced here as a destination for Christian monasticism.

deacon.description: A clerical rank in Christian churches, often assisting in liturgical services.

Jerusalem.description: A holy city in Christianity, Judaism, and Islam, significant for pilgrimage.

Holy Places.description: Sites in Jerusalem and surrounding areas considered sacred in Christianity.

Siberia.description: A vast region in Russia, often associated with exile or remote monastic missions.

Œcumenical Patriarch.description: The senior bishop and primary spiritual leader of the Eastern Orthodox Church, based in Constantinople.

Kingdom of Christ.description: A reference to the Christian belief in the future reign of Christ on earth, symbolizing an era of universal peace and justice.

consumptive.description: Suffering from tuberculosis, a common and often fatal disease in the 19th century.

epoch.description: A particular period of history or a person's life, often marked by notable events.

ascetics.description: People who practice severe self-discipline and abstention from indulgence, often for religious reasons.

cell.description: A small room in a monastery where a monk lives.

possessed with devils.description: A phrase referring to people believed to be afflicted by demonic possession.

vows of silence.description: A religious commitment to refrain from speaking for spiritual reasons.

buffoonery.description: Behavior that is ridiculous but amusing; clowning or mockery.

farce.description: A situation or event that is absurd or disorganized, often used to describe something considered a sham.

Pyotr Fomitch Kalganov.description: A young relative of Miüsov and friend of the Karamazovs who is present during the investigation and the visit to the elder.

Maximov.description: Maximov is a bald-headed, elderly landowner from Tula, a somewhat comic figure who ingratiates himself with the main characters. 'Maximushka' is an affectionate nickname for him.

Father Zossima.description: The revered and wise elder of the monastery and Alyosha's spiritual mentor, whose life and teachings influence many characters.

Father Superior.description: The Father Superior is the head of the monastery, who invites the visitors to dine with him and oversees the monastic community.

Varsonofy.description: Father Varsonofy is the previous elder of the monastery, remembered for his eccentric behavior and believed to have shown miraculous incorruptibility.

Madame Hohlakov.description: Madame Hohlakov is a prominent lady from Harkov, mother of Lise, and a central figure in the town's social life.

von Sohn.description: A person referenced by Fyodor Pavlovitch, likely a figure known for distinctive features or reputation.

late mass.description: A church service held later in the morning, after which the visitors arrive.

university of Zurich.description: A prestigious university in Switzerland, considered by Kalganov as a study destination.

Jena.description: A German university town, also mentioned as a possible destination for Kalganov.

hotel.description: The local inn where visitors to the monastery stay.

Tula.description: A city in Russia, the home region of Maximov.

copse.description: A small group of trees or a thicket, which the visitors must cross to reach the hermitage.

Harkov.description: A city in Ukraine (now Kharkiv), the origin of Madame Hohlakov.

precincts.description: The enclosed grounds of the monastery, marking the boundary between sacred and secular space.

portico.description: A covered entrance or porch area at the monastery, where women of the people wait to see the elder.

Parisian.description: A person from Paris, used here to describe Miüsov's cosmopolitan and advanced attitudes.

copeck.description: A small Russian coin, one hundredth of a rouble.

audience.description: A formal meeting or interview, especially with someone of high status.

chevalier.description: French for 'knight,' used here to mean a gentleman or chivalrous person.

saints.description: Holy persons recognized by the church, often depicted or venerated in monasteries.

sign of the cross.description: A Christian gesture of tracing a cross upon oneself, symbolizing faith and blessing.

vale of roses.description: A poetic expression for a beautiful or idyllic place.

compact.description: An agreement or pact, here referring to a promise to behave properly.

charlatanism.description: Deception or fraud, especially by pretending to have knowledge or skill.

Father Païssy.description: Father Païssy is a learned monk of the hermitage, delicate in health but not old, present in the elder's cell. Païssy Velitchkovsky is the influential monk who revived the tradition of elders in Russian monasteries, and the two are closely associated.

Rakitin.description: A cynical divinity student and intellectual who attempts to influence Alyosha and the younger boys with radical ideas.

Diderot.description: Denis Diderot, an 18th-century French philosopher and noted atheist, referenced in an anecdote.

Metropolitan Platon.description: A high-ranking Russian Orthodox bishop, mentioned in Fyodor Pavlovitch's story.

Empress Catherine.description: Catherine the Great, Empress of Russia, referenced in the anecdote about Diderot.

Princess Dashkov.description: A Russian noblewoman, mentioned as Diderot's supposed godmother in Fyodor Pavlovitch's fabricated story.

Potyomkin.description: Grigory Potemkin, a Russian statesman and favorite of Catherine the Great, mentioned as Diderot's supposed godfather.

ikon.description: A religious painting or image, especially in the Eastern Orthodox Church, venerated as sacred.

Catholic cross.description: A cross used in Roman Catholic tradition, here described as made of ivory and featuring the Mater Dolorosa.

Mater Dolorosa.description: A depiction of the Virgin Mary in her sorrow, especially as she mourns Jesus' crucifixion.

Italian artists.description: Refers to renowned painters from Italy, whose engravings are present in the elder's cell.

Russian bishops.description: Senior leaders in the Russian Orthodox Church, whose portraits are displayed in the cell.

Ispravnik.description: A local police chief or district official in pre-revolutionary Russia.

Napravnik.description: A pun on 'Ispravnik'; also refers to Eduard Nápravník, a famous Russian orchestra conductor.

Lives of the Saints.description: A collection of hagiographies, or biographies of Christian saints, widely read in Orthodox tradition.

blessing.description: A ritual act in which a religious figure invokes divine favor, often accompanied by gestures such as making the sign of the cross.

rite.description: A religious or ceremonial practice, often with prescribed actions and words.

penitence.description: The feeling or expression of remorse for one's sins, often accompanied by a desire for atonement.

engraving.description: A print made from an etched or carved plate, often used for reproducing works of art.

farthings.description: A small unit of currency, formerly used in Britain, here meaning a very small amount of money.

martyr.description: A person who suffers death or persecution for their religious beliefs.

freethinkers.description: Individuals who form opinions about religion based on reason rather than tradition or authority.

incontinence of speech.description: Lack of restraint in speaking; speaking impulsively or excessively.

taverns.description: Establishments where alcoholic drinks are served; often associated with rowdy or immoral behavior.

bestiality.description: Behavior that is brutal, depraved, or lacking in human sensibility (not the modern legal meaning).

Nastasya.description: A grieving peasant woman who has come on a pilgrimage to Father Zossima after the death of her young son.

Nikita.description: Nastasya's husband, a driver, who is mentioned as struggling with grief and drinking.

Stepanida Ilyinishna.description: A rich merchant's wife who advises another woman on religious practices regarding her missing son.

Prohorovna.description: A widow of a non-commissioned officer, seeking news and prayers for her son Vasenka who is in Irkutsk.

Vasenka.description: Prohorovna's son, serving in the commissariat in Irkutsk, Siberia, and missing for a year.

Lizaveta.description: A baby girl brought by her mother from Vyshegorye to receive Father Zossima's blessing.

monk.description: A member of a religious community, especially in the Orthodox Christian tradition.

sacrament.description: A sacred Christian rite, especially referring here to the Eucharist (Holy Communion).

Russia.description: The country in which the novel is set, providing cultural and social context.

Irkutsk.description: A city in Siberia, Russia, mentioned as the location where Vasenka is serving.

Vyshegorye.description: A village or locality near the monastery, from which a peasant woman has come.

Kingdom of Heaven.description: A Christian term referring to the afterlife or the realm of God.

Temple.description: A place of worship, here likely referring to the Jewish Temple or a church.

man of God.description: A title for a saint, specifically referring to Saint Alexey, a revered figure in Russian Orthodoxy.

commissariat.description: A military or governmental department responsible for supplies and logistics.

church.description: The church refers to the Orthodox Christian Church, central to Russian religious and social life.

service.description: A religious ceremony or liturgical event, such as the Divine Liturgy.

precinct.description: The enclosed area surrounding the monastery or church.

possessed.description: A term used for people believed to be under the influence of evil spirits, often exhibiting convulsions or strange behavior.

pilgrimage.description: A journey to a sacred place for religious reasons.

dirge.description: A mournful song or chant, often associated with funerals or lamentation.

townfolk.description: Residents of a town, as opposed to peasants from the countryside.

copecks.description: A small unit of Russian currency, one hundredth of a ruble.

stole.description: A long, narrow strip of cloth worn by clergy during religious services.

bowed down to the earth.description: A gesture of deep reverence or humility, often part of Orthodox worship.

Communion.description: The Christian sacrament of receiving the body and blood of Christ, also known as the Eucharist.

expiate.description: To atone for or make amends for guilt or sin.

non-commissioned officer.description: A military officer who has not earned a commission, typically holding a lower rank.

sing-song.description: A rhythmic, chant-like manner of speaking, often used in lamentation or folk customs.

dweller in the town.description: A phrase indicating someone who lives in the town rather than the countryside.

Lise.description: Lise Hohlakov is a young girl who is a friend of Alyosha and sends flowers for Ilusha's funeral. She is close to her mother and displays a precocious, sometimes mischievous nature.

Katerina Ivanovna.description: A noblewoman of great moral strength and pride who is engaged to Dmitri but also deeply involved with Ivan.

Doctor Herzenstube.description: The elderly local town doctor of German origin, known for his kindness and his role in various medical examinations throughout the story.

Russian.description: Refers to the people and culture of Russia, often invoked with national pride in the novel.

Obdorsk.description: A town in the far north of Russia, indicating the monk's distant origin.

Saint Sylvester.description: Likely refers to a monastery or religious community named after Saint Sylvester, a Christian saint.

sister of mercy.description: A term for a female nurse, especially one belonging to a religious order, devoted to caring for the sick and poor.

quadrille.description: A lively square dance popular in 19th-century Europe, often performed at social gatherings.

paroxysm.description: A sudden outburst of emotion or activity.

martyrs.description: People who suffer or die for their religious beliefs.

burdocks.description: A type of large, coarse weed with prickly heads, often found growing in graveyards or wastelands.

superior authorities.description: Those in higher positions of power, especially within a monastery or religious institution.

Father Iosif.description: The monastery's librarian and a monk who participates in theological discussions at the hermitage.

Europe.description: Refers to the continent, often invoked in the novel as a symbol of Western ideas and modernity.

State.description: The secular government, often contrasted with the Church in discussions of authority and morality.

ecclesiastical court.description: A court run by the Church to handle religious and moral offenses, distinct from civil courts.

Christianity.description: The religion based on the teachings of Jesus Christ, central to the novel's themes.

Roman Empire.description: The ancient empire that adopted Christianity, referenced in discussions of Church and State.

Rome.description: Refers both to the city and to the Roman Catholic Church, often contrasted with Russian Orthodoxy.

Gospel.description: The teachings of Jesus Christ as recorded in the New Testament.

On the Foundations of Church Jurisdictio.description: A book referenced in the discussion about the Church's authority and its relationship to the State.

nineteenth century.description: The time period in which the novel is set, marked by social and intellectual upheaval.

Orthodox Church.description: The Eastern Orthodox Christian Church, the dominant faith in Russia.

Government.description: Refers to the ruling administrative body, often contrasted with the Church.

Pope Gregory the Seventh.description: A medieval pope known for asserting the authority of the Roman Catholic Church over secular rulers.

coup d'état of December.description: Refers to the 1851 coup in France by Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, establishing the Second Empire.

arrière-pensée.description: A French term meaning a hidden or ulterior motive.

Ultramontanism.description: A doctrine emphasizing the supreme authority of the Pope over local churches.

excommunication.description: The formal exclusion of someone from participation in the sacraments and services of the Church.

alms.description: Charitable donations or gifts to the poor, encouraged by Christian doctrine.

secular law.description: Law that is not based on religious authority but on civil or governmental authority.

socialist.description: A person who advocates for socialism, a political and economic system where the means of production are owned collectively.

anarchist.description: A person who believes in or tries to bring about anarchy, the absence of government and absolute freedom of the individual.

infidel.description: A term used to describe someone who does not believe in a particular religion, often used pejoratively.

regiment.description: A military unit, here used to describe an organized group, such as detectives.

Katchalnikov.description: The local justice of the peace who has described Dmitri as 'of an unstable and unbalanced mind.'

Smerdyakov.description: Smerdyakov is the enigmatic valet of the Karamazov family, known for his mysterious demeanor and epileptic fits. He is sometimes mockingly called 'Æsop.'

Anna Order.description: A Russian imperial order of chivalry, awarded for distinguished service.

Karl Moor.description: A reference to the protagonist of Schiller's play 'The Robbers,' symbolizing a rebellious son.

Franz Moor.description: A reference to the villainous brother in 'The Robbers,' representing the undutiful son.

Schiller's Robbers.description: A famous German play by Friedrich Schiller about two brothers in conflict with their father.

Count von Moor.description: The father character in 'The Robbers,' invoked here as a parallel to Fyodor Pavlovitch.

Church jurisdiction.description: Refers to the authority and legal matters governed by the Russian Orthodox Church.

Alexander of Macedon.description: Another name for Alexander the Great, used here as a metaphor for greatness.

Fido.description: A common dog name, used metaphorically to describe someone meek or humble.

Karamazov.description: The family name of the main characters, central to the novel.

frock-coat.description: A formal, knee-length coat worn by men in the 19th century.

valet.description: A personal male servant, especially one who attends to the clothes and personal needs of his employer.

betrothed.description: A person to whom one is engaged to be married.

civil marriage.description: A marriage performed, recorded, and recognized by a government official rather than by a religious ceremony.

I.O.U..description: A written acknowledgment of debt ('I owe you').

parricide.description: The act of killing one's own father.

gudgeon.description: A small freshwater fish, often eaten by monks as a simple food.

dilettanti.description: People who cultivate an area of interest, such as the arts, without real commitment or knowledge.

Porfiry.description: A monk or attendant who assists Father Zossima, mentioned as being present with him.

Grushenka.description: A beautiful and enigmatic woman who is the object of both Dmitri's and Fyodor Pavlovitch's obsession; she is also referred to as a woman of authority in legal matters.

Father Isidor.description: A monk at the monastery, seen shouting after the Karamazovs during the commotion.

Pushkin.description: Alexander Pushkin, a famous Russian poet often referenced in Russian literature.

archimandrite.description: A high-ranking abbot or superior in the Eastern Orthodox Church.

Neva.description: A river running through Saint Petersburg.

bedstead.description: A bed frame, typically made of metal or wood.

felt.description: A type of fabric, here used as a mattress covering.

banquet.description: A formal, elaborate meal, often for many guests.

gypsy.description: A term (now considered pejorative) for the Romani people, often associated with itinerant lifestyles.

tavern.description: An inn or establishment where alcoholic drinks are served.

harlot.description: An archaic term for a prostitute.

poseurs.description: People who pretend to be something they are not, often to impress others.

lodgers.description: People who rent rooms in another person's house.

kitchen.description: In this context, refers to the servants' area of a grand house, where lower-status guests might be received.

Archbishop.description: A high-ranking bishop in the Orthodox Church, overseeing multiple dioceses.

Synod.description: The governing council of the Russian Orthodox Church, responsible for church doctrine and administration.

Eliseyev Brothers.description: A famous merchant family in Russia, known for their luxury food stores and products.

Karl von Moor.description: A reference to the main character in Schiller's play 'The Robbers,' used here as a mocking nickname.

Flagellants.description: A religious sect known for practicing self-flagellation as penance, referenced here to criticize monastic practices.

mead.description: An alcoholic beverage made from fermented honey and water.

kvas.description: A traditional Russian fermented beverage made from rye bread, low in alcohol.

vodka.description: A clear distilled alcoholic beverage, traditional in Russia.

sterlets.description: A small species of sturgeon fish, considered a delicacy in Russian cuisine.

compote.description: A dessert made of stewed fruit in syrup.

blanc-mange.description: A sweet, gelatinous dessert made with milk and sugar, thickened with gelatin or cornstarch.

verst.description: A Russian unit of distance, approximately 1.07 kilometers (about two-thirds of a mile).

lenten oil.description: Oil permitted for use during Lent in the Orthodox Church, when animal products are restricted.

kasha.description: A Russian dish made from boiled grains, such as buckwheat or millet.

prostrations.description: Acts of bowing or lying face down as a gesture of deep respect or worship, common in Orthodox practice.

Liberalism.description: A political and social philosophy advocating individual freedoms and reforms, referenced here as a sign of modernity.

Marfa Ignatyevna.description: Grigory's clever and prudent wife who has served the Karamazov household for many years.

Lizaveta Smerdyastchaya.description: Lizaveta Smerdyastchaya, known as 'Stinking Lizaveta,' is a mute, mentally disabled woman who gives birth to Smerdyakov in the bath-house.

Karamazovs.description: The family at the center of the novel, consisting of Fyodor Pavlovitch and his sons.

Miüsov family.description: A wealthy family in whose service Marfa once worked as a servant and dancer.

Book of Job.description: A book from the Old Testament of the Bible, which Grigory reads for spiritual comfort.

Father Isaac the Syrian.description: A revered Christian monk and theologian whose sayings and sermons Grigory reads.

Lent.description: A significant period of fasting and penitence in the Christian calendar, during which Grigory reads aloud.

lodge.description: A separate building on the estate where the servants live and cooking is done.

emancipation of the serfs.description: The 1861 reform in Russia that freed the serfs from bondage to landowners.

font.description: A basin or receptacle in a church used for baptism.

the Russian Dance.description: A traditional Russian folk dance, distinct from village dancing, often performed with professional instruction.

christening.description: The Christian sacrament of baptism, especially as performed on infants.

Ilya.description: Lizaveta's father, a homeless and sickly drunkard who abused his daughter and worked for tradespeople after losing everything.

Karp.description: A dangerous convict who had escaped from prison and was suspected by some townspeople of being Lizaveta's abuser.

Kondratyev.description: A well-to-do merchant's widow who took Lizaveta into her house to care for her during her pregnancy.

cathedral.description: A principal church in the town, often the center of religious and community life in Russian towns.

governor.description: The official appointed to oversee a province in Imperial Russia, responsible for local administration.

civil councilor.description: A rank in the Russian civil service, indicating a respected official of significant standing.

Fyodorovitch.description: A Russian patronymic meaning 'son of Fyodor,' used as part of Smerdyakov's full name.

hempen smock.description: A simple, coarse garment made from hemp, typically worn by peasants or the poor.

alms-jug.description: A container placed in churches or public places for collecting donations for the poor.

farthing.description: A very small amount of money; originally a British coin, used here to mean a trivial sum.

hurdle.description: A woven fence or barrier, often used in rural Russia instead of wooden fences.

confinement.description: The period of childbirth or the time when a woman is expected to give birth.

midwife.description: A woman trained to assist in childbirth.

crape.description: A black, crinkled fabric worn as a sign of mourning.

von Schmidt.description: Von Schmidt is a retired colonel who formerly owned the house adjoining Fyodor Pavlovitch's property.

High Street.description: The main street in the town, often the commercial or central thoroughfare.

Ceres.description: In Roman mythology, the goddess of agriculture, referenced here in connection with poetry about man and the earth.

Silenus.description: A figure from Greek mythology, companion of Dionysus, often depicted as drunken and wise.

Sodom.description: A biblical city destroyed for its wickedness, symbolizing moral depravity.

name-day.description: A Russian tradition celebrating the feast day of the saint after whom a person is named, often marked with festivities.

jade.description: An archaic term for a disreputable or flirtatious woman.

arbor.description: A small shelter made of latticework or branches, often found in gardens.

hundredweight.description: A unit of weight equal to 100 pounds (in British usage) or 112 pounds (in some contexts); here, it refers to the amount of hay harvested.

decay.description: Decomposition of a body after death.

cannon.description: A toy cannon, significant as a cherished possession of Ilusha.

crossed.description: In this context, refers to land that has been blessed or consecrated by the sign of the cross.

automaton.description: A person acting in a mechanical or emotionless way, used to describe the mother's grief-stricken movements.

candlestick.description: A holder for candles, used during the funeral service.

wreath.description: A circular arrangement of flowers, often used in funerals.

rites.description: Religious or ceremonial acts, here referring to the burial customs.

grave-diggers.description: People employed to dig graves for burials.

crust.description: A piece of bread, here used in the custom of crumbling bread on a grave for birds.

pancakes.description: A traditional Russian food (blini) often served at funeral dinners.

funeral prayers.description: Prayers recited for the soul of the deceased during the funeral service.
